chunks: Ibn Ayyash mentioned: One day I was with Abu Dalf, and we began mentioning Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi.
He said to me: Do you know from where the superiority of our master, the Shaykh, may Allah sanctify his soul, and he was sanctified through him over Abul Qasim Husayn ibn Ruh and others?
I said to him: I do not know. He said: Because Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Uthman mentioned his name before his name in his will.
He said: So I said to him: Then Mansur is superior to our master Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him).
He said: How? I said: Because al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) mentioned his name before his name in the will.
He said to me: You are biased towards our master and you hate him.
I said: All of creation hates Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi and is biased against him, except you alone.
We were about to fight each other and grab each other by the collars.

The matter of Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi regarding his lack of knowledge and nobility is more famous, and the madness of Abu Dalf is more than can be counted. We will not occupy our book with that nor prolong mentioning it. And Ibn Nuh mentioned some of it.

key_terms.أَبُو الْقَاسِمِ الْحُسَيْنُ بْنُ رَوْحٍ: Abul Qasim Husayn ibn Ruh, the third deputy
key_terms.أَبُو بَكْرٍ الْبَغْدَادِيُّ: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, the fourth deputy of the Twelfth Imam
key_terms.أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عُثْمَانَ: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Uthman, the fourth deputy
key_terms.أَبُو دَلْفٍ: Abu Dalf, a contemporary figure known for his eccentricities
key_terms.الْوَصِيَّةُ: The will/testament, used here as evidence for hierarchical status

ai.seo_question: How did Abu Dalf justify the superiority of Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi over other Imami deputies?
ai.summary: This anecdote from *Kitab al-Ghayba* illustrates the early Shia scholarly debate over the criteria for the 'Superior Deputy' (*al-Shaykh al-Akbar*), specifically critiquing the reliance on mere chronological precedence in a will (*wasiyya*) as a marker of spiritual rank. Abu Dalf’s argument that Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi’s superiority is evidenced by being named first in Muhammad ibn Uthman’s will is challenged by Ibn Ayyash, who exposes the potential for bias by applying the same logic to the Imam al-Sadiq’s relationship with Musa al-Kazim. The passage highlights the tension between political favor and genuine scholarly merit, noting that while Abu Bakr was widely revered, his critics argued his elevation was partly due to his own influence and the exclusion of rivals.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: H 387 - Ibn Ayyash mentioned: One day I was with Abu Dalf. We mentioned Abu Bakr Baghdadi.
He said: “Do you know how our master, the Shaykh, may Allah bless his soul, was great?” He made Abu Bakr Baghdadi higher than Abul Qasim Husain Ibn Rauh and others.
I said: “I don’t know.” He said: “Because Abu Ja’far Muhammad Ibn Uthman mentioned his name before the name of Abul Qasim Husain in his final will.”
I said to him, “On this account, then Mansur must be higher than our master Imam Abul Hasan Musa (a.s).”
He said: “How?” I said: “Because Imam Sadiq (a.s) mentioned Mansur’s name before his successor in his final will.”
He said: “You are biased about our master and you hate him.”
I said: “All of the creation hates Abu Bakr Baghdadi and dislike him, except only you.”
We were about to start fighting and hold each other’s collars.

Abu Bakr Baghdadi’s ignorance and lack of nobility is well-known. Abu Dalf’s stories of madness are more than to be accounted for. We will not engage our book with them. Ibn Nuh has mentioned some of them.
